description: We are FLYING WOMEN, an all-female team of young innovators aged 17–18 connected through high school, university, and events, dedicated to designing an interactive simulation that balances real-world NASA engineering trade-offs while actively promoting female empowerment in STEM to inspire the next generation of young women to see themselves as future mission directors and space engineers.
summary:
C.A.S.C.L.E. (Cosmics And Space Capacities Learning Experience) is an educational lunar base simulator for children aged 7–12. Players manage a crew of four women scientists and must keep oxygen, power, water, plants and radiation shielding safe for 28 Sols. It is a playable browser game with nothing to install: time moves, resources change, and players face a greenhouse irrigation problem, a timed solar storm decision and the 14-day lunar night, with a tablet to track stats and crew health.

The challenge asks for space education that is both accurate and accessible. C.A.S.C.L.E. teaches real trade-offs through play. Every choice, such as sending the crew to the bunker or activating shields, has a scientific cost based on NASA data. Each event starts with a simple, kid-friendly explanation, and the game slows down so children can read before they act.

This matters because children who understand how a life support system works may be inspired to pursue STEM careers. Female empowerment is central to the project: every badge honours a real woman in science or spaceflight, such as Judith Love Cohen, Dr. Gioia Massa, Christina Koch and Peggy Whitson, so young players see themselves in these roles.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

C.A.S.C.L.E. (Cosmics And Space Capacities Learning Experience) is an educational lunar base simulator for children aged 7–12. The player runs a base with four astronauts for 28 Sols (lunar days) and must keep oxygen, power, water, plants, radiation shielding and crew health safe.

C.A.S.C.L.E. is a playable browser game. It runs in any modern browser, with no installation and no account.

  • Play now: https://nottolaspaziale.github.io/CASCLE/

Time really moves in the game, resources change every second, and events trigger during the mission. The game is built from the team's Figma prototype (https://cascleflyingwomen.carrd.co/). The original screens, art and texts are now one connected game.

  • Sol 1, Astronaut Management: move the crew around the base and give each astronaut role-based actions.
  • Sol 4, Greenhouse Problem: a plant irrigation emergency that the player must fix.
  • Sol 8, Solar Emergency: a solar storm alert and a timed choice.
  • Sol 14, Lunar Night: 14 days of darkness, survived on battery power alone.
  • Tablet: stats, tasks, badges and crew health, available at any time.

Every event opens with a short, kid-friendly explanation based on real NASA data before the player must act. When an alert appears, the game slows back to normal speed and pauses, so children have time to read.

Time and speed

One Sol lasts 5 real minutes at 1x speed. Clicking the SOL button opens a speed menu (1x, 2x, 4x, 10x) and a pause button. At 10x, a full mission takes about 14 minutes.

The crew

The four astronauts were named with AI-generated names:

  • Luana Santos, Lunar Geologist: focus on the Geology Lab, lunar regolith sample analysis, and surface EVA expeditions.
  • Maya Brooks, Space Biologist: focus on the Hydroponic Greenhouse (Veggie/APH), crop hydration, LED light schedules, and fresh food harvests.
  • Astrid Lindqvist, Systems and Power Engineer: focus on the Life Support System (ECLSS), O₂/CO₂ scrubbers, water recycling, and the base power panel.
  • Hannah Becker, Flight Surgeon: focus on the Medical Bay, vital signs, radiation exposure checks, and fitness monitoring.

Each astronaut appears on the hand-drawn base map as a face icon. Clicking an icon opens a radial menu of rooms. Choosing a room shows its actions, for example Sleep 8h, Eat Meal, Lift Weights (ARED), Clean Air Filters (CDRA) or Call Earth. The astronaut then glides through the corridor to that room and performs the action.

  • Common actions for all crew: eat, drink, sleep, exercise, socialize, medical check-up.
  • Role-specific actions: marked with a ★. Specialists finish their own tasks faster and with better results.

Every astronaut has needs that change over time: hunger, hydration, sleep, fatigue, mood, stress, radiation, bone mass and muscle mass. A small warning dot on the icon shows when someone needs attention. Socializing works better when two or more astronauts meet in the Galley.

Sol 4: Greenhouse problem

  • A "!" icon appears on the labs. The Veggie sensors report low water in the plant pillows, and the game explains why water behaves differently in low gravity.
    1. Water the plants by hand. This costs water and energy. The button then needs a short cooldown, because plants need time to recover.
    2. Send Maya, the biologist, to manage the greenhouse. She keeps the plants watered automatically, but she gets tired. The player must balance the crew's workload against manual work.
  • Saving the greenhouse unlocks the Greenhouse badge with Dr. Gioia Massa as the role model (+10% crop growth).

Sol 8: Solar emergency

  • The DONKI satellite system detects a solar storm, and the game explains Solar Energetic Particles. A 30-second timer starts.
    1. Evacuate to the bunker. The crew is fully protected, but research and the greenhouse stop. The game skips 1 Sol while the crew is in the bunker, and the labs are blocked for that time. The player earns the Solar badge with Judith Love Cohen as the role model.
    2. Activate the magnetic shields. The astronauts keep working in the lab modules, so science finishes on time. This costs 30 kW of battery power and raises each astronaut's radiation by 15%. The mission continues with this higher risk.
  • If the player does not choose in time, the crew is exposed to the storm without protection, their health drops fast, and the mission fails.
  • On Hard, the shields only work if the Radiation Shield is powered on in the power panel.
  • Smaller space weather alerts (solar flares and CMEs) can appear on other days with fun facts, such as the 1859 solar storm and auroras on Earth.

Sol 14: Lunar night

  • The "!" icon appears on the Life Support System. Tapping it explains that the Moon has 14 days of sunlight and 14 days of darkness. During darkness, the solar panels produce 0%, and the base lives on its 1000-unit battery.
    • Easy: the player uses three buttons, ALL MAX, ALL ECO and ALL OFF.
    • Hard: the player sets every system individually. Crew-safety systems cannot go below ECO.
  • Reaching Sol 28 with power left wins the mission and unlocks two badges: Power Management (Christina Koch) and 28 Sol Achievement (Peggy Whitson).

Win and lose

  • Win: reach Sol 28 with power left.
  • Lose: the mission fails if power, oxygen, water, shielding or plant health reaches zero, if any astronaut's health reaches zero, or if the crew is left unprotected during a solar storm.
  • On failure, the screen turns black and white and explains the cause, and START AGAIN restarts from Sol 1.

The tablet menu

A tablet button in the top bar opens the menu at any time and pauses the game. It has four sections:

  • Stats: live oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, solar panel output, battery and shields, with their hourly change.
  • Tasks: each astronaut's daily routine, with a full-body avatar and the current activity highlighted.
  • Badges: the four badges, locked or unlocked, each with its unlock condition, role model and bonus.
  • Crew Health: each astronaut's physical status (radiation, bone mass, muscle mass), energy and fatigue (sleep, fatigue, hunger, hydration) and mental state (mood and stress). Every value has Fix and Ignore buttons. Fix sends the astronaut to the right room, for example the Galley to eat or the Gym to exercise. Ignore hides the warning until the next Sol, and the problem keeps getting worse.

Sound

Simple sound effects play for alerts, the storm countdown, watering, badges, victory and failure. A mute button is always visible.

Tip for judges: add ?sol=N to the link to jump to any Sol:

  • Greenhouse: https://nottolaspaziale.github.io/CASCLE/?sol=4
  • Solar storm: https://nottolaspaziale.github.io/CASCLE/?sol=8
  • Lunar night: https://nottolaspaziale.github.io/CASCLE/?sol=14

Future features

  • A Medium difficulty level, between Easy (all-room buttons) and Hard (every system).
  • Control of each individual piece of equipment.
  • More lunar cycles, with new events and new badges.
  • Touch and tablet-friendly controls.

Tools used

  • Figma: the whole UI design and the original linked prototype.
  • Photoshop and ibisPaint: the hand-drawn lunar base map.
  • Canva: the badges (using free templates from the site) and the presentation template.
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript: the browser game. It has no frameworks, no build step and no database.
  • Claude Code (AI coding assistant): helped turn the Figma prototype into the playable game and test it automatically in the browser.
  • ChatGPT (AI research assistant): helped find useful data through NASA documentation.
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages: version control and free online hosting.
  • NASA open data: the ISS, DONKI, OSDR, and plant experiment datasets.

Creativity

  • Familiar style: the character movement and base management are inspired by The Sims, Among Us, Habbo and Good Pizza, Great Pizza.
  • Real science as gameplay: the events (solar storms, the lunar night, plant irrigation) come from real NASA facts, and the player's choices decide the outcome.
  • Trade-offs, not right answers: the bunker keeps the crew safe but stops research and the greenhouse. The shields keep work and plants going but put the crew at risk. Sending Maya to the greenhouse saves effort but tires her out.
  • Role models: each badge honours a real woman in science or spaceflight.

Factors the team considered

  • Age-appropriate design: the language is simple, the game explains each event before asking the player to act, and every alert slows the game down so children can read.
  • Scientific accuracy: the team used real NASA data, and simplified values are labelled as game values.
  • Clear first-time experience: the title screen explains the mission, the three main dangers and how to play.
  • Crew of four: all calculations use four astronauts.
  • Accessible: it runs in any browser with nothing to install, and children can start playing right away.
